memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text:
"'No person devoted to destruction may be ransomed; they are to be put to
death'" - Lev 27:29 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is a hard and sobering verse, and we must handle it honestly rather
than rush past it. It refers to persons or things placed under God's
irreversible judgment — most likely those condemned under the specific
judicial sentences of Israel's covenant law, such as those set apart for
destruction after warnings had gone unheeded.

We should be clear about what this is not. This was part of the civil and
covenant law given to Israel as a nation at a particular moment in
redemptive history. It is not a licence or pattern for how anyone today
should treat other people. Jesus explicitly forbade His followers from
calling down destruction on others (Luke 9:54-55).

But we must let the verse do its proper work. It reminds us that God's
judgment is real, and that there are points beyond which persistent,
hardened rebellion cannot simply be undone. Scripture does not present a
God who is endlessly indifferent to evil.

And yet — here is the wonder of the gospel — the very word that stands out
in this verse is "ransomed." What could not be ransomed under this law
points, by sharp contrast, to what Christ has done. Jesus said the Son of
Man came to give His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Paul says
there is one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom
for all (1 Tim 2:6).

The law shows us the seriousness of judgment. The cross shows us how far
God went to provide a ransom where none seemed possible.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do I take the reality of God's judgment seriously?
2. How does the word "ransom" here point me to Christ?
3. Have I received the ransom Christ paid on my behalf?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Holy God, thank You that where no ransom seemed possible, Jesus gave
Himself as a ransom for me. I take Your judgment seriously and rest wholly
in Your mercy. Amen.
